q: What is marshaling in heraldry?
How are multiple coats of arms combined on one shield?
What is impalement in heraldry?
What is quartering in heraldic marshaling?
What is dimidiation in heraldry?
What is tiercing in heraldry?
What is an escutcheon of pretense?
heraldic marshaling impalement quartering dimidiation tiercing en surtout
a: Marshaling is the technique of combining two or more coats of arms on a single shield to represent marriage, inheritance, offices held, or territorial claims. The most common methods are impalement (dividing the shield vertically, placing one coat in each half, typically used for married couples) and quartering (dividing the shield into four or more sections to display inherited arms from multiple heiress ancestors). Dimidiation is an older, less common method where only half of each coat is shown, cut vertically, while escutcheon of pretense places a small shield of one's inherited or claimed arms in the center of another shield, commonly used by husbands of heraldic heiresses.

q: What is cadency in heraldry?
How are younger sons distinguished from the eldest in heraldry?
What are the marks of cadency?
What is the label mark of cadency?
What are the cadency marks for second through ninth sons?
How are the marks of cadency arranged on a shield?

cadency fleur-de-lis rose cross moline double quatrefoil differencing
a: Cadency is the system of marks added to a coat of arms to distinguish the branches of a family descended from the same original armiger. The eldest son bears a label (a horizontal bar with three downward-pointing tags), which he removes upon inheriting his father's arms. Younger sons bear specific marks: crescent for the second son, mullet (five-pointed star) for the third, martlet (a footless bird resembling a swallow) for the fourth, annulet (ring) for the fifth, fleur-de-lis for the sixth, rose for the seventh, cross moline for the eighth, and double quatrefoil for the ninth son. These marks are typically placed in the chief (upper portion) of the shield and form part of the permanent difference for that cadet line.

q: How does Scottish differencing work compared to English cadency?

Scottish versus English cadency differencing systems
a: Scottish heraldry employs a differencing system distinct from English cadency: instead of small symbols (marks of cadency), Scottish cadets typically add a bordure (a border around the shield) of varying tinctures and patterns (wavy, indented, engrailed, or invected) to distinguish their arms from the chief's. The Lord Lyon King of Arms regulates all Scottish arms closely, and each cadet branch must apply for a formal matriculation of their differenced arms in the Public Register. This system creates clear visual differentiation between clan branches and avoids the confusion that can arise when multiple generations use the same English-style marks of cadency simultaneously.

q: How is marshaling done for married couples, widows, and widowers?
What are the marshaling rules for married couples in heraldry?
How do widows and widowers display their arms?
How are ecclesiastical arms marshaled?
What is marshaling for peeresses and ladies?
How are arms of office marshaled?

a: During marriage, a husband impales his arms with his wife's (or places her arms on an inescutcheon of pretense if she is an heraldic heiress). A widow displays her late husband's arms impaled with her own on a lozenge (diamond shape), while a widower continues impalement but may place his arms alone in dexter. Ecclesiastical arms (bishops, archbishops, dioceses) are marshaled by impalement: the personal arms of the office-holder impaling the arms of the see or diocese. Arms of office (for officials like mayors, governors, or university chancellors) may be marshaled with personal arms during tenure, then revert to personal arms alone after the term ends.
